findings.title: Removed fail-fast for multiple crypto providers; equal-order providers now resolved silently
findings.body:
`detectProvider` used to throw when more than one `CryptoProvider` was on the classpath. It now sorts by `order()` and silently returns the first one, logging the rest only at DEBUG.

`DefaultCryptoProvider`, `FIPS1402Provider` and `WildFlyElytronProvider` all return the same order (200). If two of them end up on the classpath (for example default and fips1402), the choice now depends on ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order. A FIPS setup can silently fall back to the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider, or the reverse, with no visible warning.

It gets worse because ServiceLoader instantiates every provider before sorting. The constructors of the "ignored" providers still run their global side effects: `Security.addProvider(BC)`, and `insertProviderAt` of KeycloakFipsSecurityProvider/BCFIPS/BCJSSE plus `ssl.*ManagerFactory.algorithm` property changes. Previously that misconfiguration made startup fail. Now the JVM keeps running with mixed security-provider state.

The ordering should only be used to break ties between different priorities. If several providers share the highest order it should still throw, or at least log a WARN.

findings.title: New abstract `order()` breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations (source and binary)
findings.body:
`int order()` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` SPI as an abstract method.

Any third-party or extension implementation of `CryptoProvider` no longer compiles. Worse, an implementation compiled against the previous keycloak-common will throw `AbstractMethodError` at runtime when `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` calls `CryptoProvider::order` in the comparator. That error surfaces during crypto initialization and breaks startup.

This should be a `default` method returning a sensible base value, so existing implementations keep working and only the providers that need a different priority override it.

findings.title: ES384/ES512 tests use a P-256 key and only check self-round-trip
findings.body:
The key pair comes from `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, which uses the JDK default curve (P-256). `testES384` and `testES512` therefore sign with a P-256 key, so r and s are always about 32 bytes and are just zero-padded to 48/66.

A real ES512 (P-521) signature has a DER SEQUENCE body over 127 bytes. That requires the long-form length encoding in `ASN1Encoder.writeLength` and the long-form parsing in `ASN1Decoder.readLength`, and neither path is ever exercised.

The assertion is also weak. It only checks that decode → encode → decode through the same new code is self-consistent. It never compares the re-encoded DER with the original `sign` bytes (DER is canonical, so they should be identical), and it never verifies the signature with `Signature.verify`. A symmetric bug in the encoder and decoder would pass.

The test should generate keys on the matching curve (secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) and assert `assertArrayEquals(sign, asn1Des)` and/or verify the re-encoded signature.

findings.title: Leftover dead code in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: Lines 114-115 (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger); ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);`) build two encoders and throw the results away. The real encoding is done again on lines 117-121. This is leftover code that adds allocations on every signature conversion and should be removed.
